title: Beacon was a small square of dark in a black room
thesis: A game about light was rendering almost none of it — and was doing so inside a 780-pixel box with the rest of the screen painted black.
summary: Beacon asks you to identify ships by their silhouette as a lighthouse beam sweeps them, then flash the right signal. The idea was sound; the presentation was not. The playfield was a fixed square that used barely half the window, ships were flat grey cut-outs floating above the horizon, and the lighthouse was a triangle with two circles on top. It is now a full-width sea with a moon, a swell that carries light, and ships that show the running lights the whole game is about.

comparisons.title: The watch used barely half the window
comparisons.caption: Both frames are the same moment of the same wave at 1440×900. The old build sized its canvas to a square of min(innerWidth, innerHeight − 120, 900) — 780×780 here — and centred it, so roughly 46% of the width was painted black and it never grew past 900px however large your display. The field is now the window, and the sea runs to both edges.

before.alt: Beacon before: a small square playfield centred in a wide black frame, with a faint lighthouse and two pale ship shapes.

after.alt: Beacon after: a full-width moonlit sea with a layered swell, a lighthouse on its rock, and several ships at different distances.

comparisons.title: The light had nothing to fall on
comparisons.caption: Same crop of the approach, enlarged. Before: ships hung above the horizon line because the field was a flat disc rather than a sea surface, the beam was one translucent wedge laid over the dark, and the swell was ten identical sine lines. After: the field is squashed into a ground plane so vessels ride the water, the beam is three stacked wedges that re-light every wave crest they cross, and each ship carries red-to-port, green-to-starboard and masthead-white lamps — the signals the game is named for.

before.alt: Detail before: flat grey ship silhouettes above the horizon, a plain translucent beam wedge, and a lighthouse drawn as a triangle with a circle.

after.alt: Detail after: a tapered banded lighthouse with gallery railing and glowing lantern on a rock ringed by surf, with the beam lighting individual wave crests.

changes.title: The canvas became the window
changes.body: resize() built a square from min(innerWidth, innerHeight − 120, 900). Width and height are now independent and the canvas fills the viewport at every size — verified at 390×844, 768×1024, 1440×900 and 1920×1080, including resizing mid-game. Every gameplay distance was re-expressed as a fraction of a play radius rather than of the canvas edge, so the rules did not change when the frame did.

changes.title: The disc became a sea
changes.body: Ships approach the lighthouse on a bearing, and the field was drawn as a flat circle — so a ship due north was painted in the sky. The field is now squashed vertically into a ground plane bounded by the horizon, and the beam, the rock ring and the fog take the same squash, so light still visibly falls on the vessels it is lighting.

changes.title: The beam lands on the water
changes.body: It was a single translucent wedge sitting over the dark. It is now a hot core, the beam proper and a wide haze scatter — and, clipped to the wedge, every wave crest inside it is re-stroked in the beam's own colour. That last part is what stops the light hovering above the sea like coloured paper.

changes.title: Ships carry the lights the game is about
changes.body: Vessels were single flat fills. They now have hull shading from deck to waterline, a wavering reflection beneath them, a wake, and running lights — red to port, green to starboard, white at the masthead. In a game whose whole verb is signalling with coloured light, the ships not carrying any was the strangest omission of all.

changes.title: The keeper is allowed to learn
changes.body: The instruction faded after six seconds whether or not you had understood it; it now stays until your first successful rescue. And a ship the beam has already identified leaves a faint silhouette instead of vanishing back into the dark for the rest of the sweep — the beam still does the revealing, but knowledge, once earned, is no longer erased every rotation.

builderNote.quote: Are you actually happy with that result? That needs something way beyond what you did.
builderNote.context: The owner's response to the first attempt, which resized the canvas, fixed the projection, and stopped there — a correctly proportioned version of the same flat picture, presented as an improvement. It was not one. The art pass above is the second attempt: sky, sea, light, structure and vessels, rather than layout arithmetic.

proof.label: Field
proof.value: 780×780 of a 1440×900 window before (46% of the width unused); the full viewport after.

proof.label: Responsive
proof.value: Canvas fills the window at 390×844, 768×1024, 1440×900 and 1920×1080, and survives two resizes mid-game.

proof.label: Errors
proof.value: Zero page or console errors across every viewport and a full wave played out.

proof.label: Still open
proof.value: Ship silhouettes are still simple polygons; weather and sea state do not yet change with the wave.

share.summary: A game about light was rendering almost none of it, inside a 780-pixel box with the rest of the screen painted black. See the sea it turned into.
